q: Explain why writing the same step out on many separate lines is not a sustainable substitute for repetition — say precisely what breaks as the problem scales.
notes: A full answer explains that copying the step fixes the number of executions at write time, so the algorithm is bound to one particular input size; if the data grows, the algorithm itself must be rewritten, which contradicts the requirement that an algorithm should have a limited and countable number of instructions that nonetheless handles the general problem. It also multiplies the maintenance cost: a change to the step must be made in every copy, and each copy is a chance to introduce an inconsistency, which works against maintainability and correctness. Repetition instead binds the number of executions to a condition evaluated at run time, so one written step covers any input size, and the count of instructions stays finite regardless of n.
answer: Copying the step out on separate lines fixes the number of executions at the moment the algorithm is written, and that is precisely what breaks. The algorithm stops being a solution to the general problem and becomes a solution to one particular input size: write five lines to process five marks and it is correct for exactly five marks. Give it a class of forty and the algorithm itself has to be edited before it will work, which contradicts what an algorithm is supposed to be, since a set of steps that must be rewritten whenever the data changes size has not really solved the problem at all. It also breaks the requirement that an algorithm consist of a limited and countable number of instructions, because the number of written instructions now grows in step with n: a thousand items means a thousand lines. And the maintenance cost multiplies. If the step is later corrected, the correction has to be applied to every copy, every copy is another opportunity to get it wrong, and the copy that is missed leaves the algorithm quietly inconsistent with itself, which is a correctness problem and not merely an untidiness. Repetition removes all of this by binding the number of executions to a condition evaluated while the algorithm runs rather than to what was typed, so a single written step covers any input size and the written instruction count stays fixed however large n becomes.
why: Names what breaks as the problem scales: executions fixed at write time, algorithm bound to one input size and needing rewriting, instruction count no longer finite relative to n, plus duplicated maintenance.

answer: Repetition is one of the fundamental representation forms available to an algorithm designer, standing alongside sequence and selection, and it exists precisely because writing a step out repeatedly on separate lines is not a sustainable way to express an algorithm. An algorithm rendered as a long column of identical statements is unwieldy, inelegant and hard for a reader to follow, and it obscures the structure of the solution: the reader cannot see at a glance that a single operation is being applied over and over, because the repetition has been buried in the transcription instead of being expressed in the notation itself. Good practice therefore favours a repetition construct, which captures the designer's intent directly and makes the algorithm largely self-documenting, so that anyone reading it later understands not merely what happens but why it happens that way. Duplication of this sort has long been recognised as poor style in both algorithm design and programming, and much of the discipline exists to give us better tools than plain transcription. The repeated-line approach should accordingly be regarded as a failure of expression rather than as a genuine alternative to repetition, and a well-designed algorithm will always use a repetition construct wherever a step has to be carried out more than once.

q: Explain why a heuristic is a sound choice for picking a brand of rice in a shop but an unsound one for deciding how much money Dan gave away, given the two things a heuristic trades against each other.
notes: A heuristic buys a fast decision at the cost of any guarantee that the result is rational or optimal, so it is sound exactly where a sub-optimal answer is acceptable. Choosing a brand of rice is such a case: the cost of a slightly worse choice is trivial, and the time saved by not comparing every brand is worth more than the accuracy given up. How much money Dan gave away is not: an exact algorithm exists, the question demands the exact figure, and 'about 200' is simply wrong. The trade is only worth making when the loss on the accuracy side is one you can afford.
answer: A heuristic trades away any guarantee that the result is optimal, or even rational, and receives speed of decision in exchange. Those are the two sides of it, so a heuristic is a sound choice exactly where a sub-optimal outcome costs you little. Picking a brand of rice is that case. There may be thirty brands on the shelf, and comparing every one of them on price, weight, grain and reputation would take longer than the entire errand, while the penalty for going home with the second-best bag is close to nothing, since you will eat it and be perfectly satisfied. So 'take the one I bought last time' is a good way to decide: the accuracy you surrender is worth less to you than the time you keep. Deciding how much money Dan gave away is not that case. An exact procedure exists for it, the question asks for the exact figure and for nothing else, and an answer of 'about two hundred' is not a slightly inferior answer but simply a wrong one. Speed buys you nothing here, because the accuracy being sold is the whole of what the answer is for. The rule separating the two is therefore whether the loss on the accuracy side is a loss you can afford.
why: States both sides of the trade (speed gained, guarantee of an optimal or rational result given up) and applies it correctly to each case: trivial cost of error for the rice, exact figure demanded for Dan.

q: Write out, in C, a structure LibraryBook with the members char title[40], char author[40] and int copies. Then write the statements that create one such variable, set all three members and print the title and the number of copies, using the correct syntax for each member's type. Say what the size of the structure is and how you worked it out. Then say exactly what would change, in the layout and in the behaviour of your statements, if struct were replaced by union, and what the size would become.
notes: THE CODE: 'struct LibraryBook { char title[40]; char author[40]; int copies; };' - note the semicolon after the closing brace. Then 'struct LibraryBook b;' defines a variable and reserves the storage; 'strcpy(b.title, "Things Fall Apart"); strcpy(b.author, "Chinua Achebe"); b.copies = 3;' set the members; 'printf("%s: %d copies\n", b.title, b.copies);' prints them. TWO POINTS OF SYNTAX: the dot is how a member is reached for both reading and writing, exactly as the deck's slide says - 'to access members of a structure to either assign or modify values, use the dot syntax' - and the two char arrays cannot be set with = because an array name is not something you can store into, so their contents are copied in with strcpy, while copies, being a plain int, takes an ordinary assignment. The conversion specifiers follow the member types: %s for the arrays, %d for the int. SIZE: 40 + 40 + 4 = 84 bytes. Each member of a structure has its own storage laid out in order, so the size of the structure is the sum of its members' sizes - the same arithmetic that makes the summary sheet's struct Dog, with three char[20] members, 60 bytes. IF struct BECAME union: the layout collapses. All three members would start at the same location, so title, author and copies would be three names for one block rather than three blocks, and the size would become 40 - the size of the largest member, char[40] - because a union is big enough for its largest member and no bigger. The statements would then be destructive: strcpy(b.title, ...) writes the title at the start of the block; strcpy(b.author, ...) writes over the same place, destroying it; and b.copies = 3 writes an integer over the first bytes of that text. The printf would print rubbish for the title and 3 for the copies, because copies was written last. A union variable can represent the value of only one member at a time, so a LibraryBook - which needs a title AND an author AND a count simultaneously - must be a structure; a union is right only where the members are alternatives that never coexist.
why: Gives the declaration, the variable, the three assignments with strcpy for the arrays and = for the int, the correct %s/%d printf, the size 84 with the sum-of-members reasoning, and the union's shared layout, destructive behaviour and 40-byte size.

The dog example works by asking what a dog is and what a dog does: its state lives in variables such as name, breed and colour, and its behaviour is described by methods such as one that returns the dog's name. Variables (the state): title and author, both character data; a catalogue number that identifies the copy in the library's records; copies_owned, an integer count of how many the library has; and copies_out, an integer count of how many are currently lent. q: In her result d³y/dx³ = −125 cos(5x) + 27e^(3x), explain why the exponential term is positive while the trigonometric term carries a minus sign.
notes: A good answer separates the two terms. For e^(3x): d(eˣ)/dx = eˣ, so the exponential reproduces itself exactly and the only thing each differentiation adds is a chain factor 3 — 3, 9, 27 — all positive, and no differentiation can ever introduce a minus. For sin(5x): the derivatives cycle sin → cos → −sin → −cos, so a sign appears at the second differentiation and is still there at the third; combined with the chain factors this gives 5 cos(5x), then −25 sin(5x), then −125 cos(5x). The answer should draw the moral: the minus belongs to the trigonometric term alone, and writing −125 cos(5x) − 27e^(3x) applies it to a term that can never be negative for real x.
answer:
The two terms behave differently because the two functions behave differently under differentiation.

Take e^(3x) first. The exponential is the function that reproduces itself: d(eᵘ)/dx = eᵘ · u′, so differentiating e^(3x) hands back e^(3x) again, multiplied only by the factor 3 coming down from the inside. Repeating this gives 3e^(3x), then 9e^(3x), then 27e^(3x). Every factor introduced is +3, so the coefficient runs 3 → 9 → 27, all positive. There is no stage at which a minus can enter, because the differentiation rule for the exponential contains no minus anywhere in it.

Now sin(5x). Its derivatives run round a cycle of four: sin → cos → −sin → −cos. The minus enters at the second differentiation, when d(cos)/dx = −sin, and it is still present at the third. Carrying the factor 5 as well: the first derivative is 5cos(5x), the second −25 sin(5x), the third −125 cos(5x). The 125 is 5³ and is positive; the minus is inherited from the cycle, not from the 5.

So the minus belongs to the trigonometric term alone. Writing −125 cos(5x) − 27e^(3x) would attach it to a term that cannot be negative for any real x, since its coefficient is built out of positive threes only.
why: Explains both required halves: exponential reproduces itself with only positive factors so no minus can arise; the trig minus comes from the sin → cos → −sin → −cos cycle at the second differentiation and persists to the third.

q: Given a limit you have never seen before, describe the decision procedure the deck teaches for choosing a method, in the order she teaches them.
notes: A good answer runs the four methods in her order and ties each to a visible feature. First always substitute (slide 4): if the result is a well-defined expression, however negative or fractional, that is the answer and you stop — slide 5 exists to make that point. If substitution gives 0/0, look at what the expression is made of. Polynomials: factor, cancel the common factor, substitute again (slide 6). A small fraction inside the big one: multiply numerator and denominator by the common denominator, then factor out −1 if the cancelling bracket comes out reversed (slide 7). A square root: multiply by the conjugate of the numerator (slides 9, 10). And for 0/0 or ∞/∞ that these do not clear — including anything with sin x or eˣ in it — replace f/g by f′/g′ and re-check the form after each application (slides 12, 13). A strong answer adds that the slide 11 TASK needs two of these at once, and that agreement between two methods is a free check on the answer.
answer:
Her procedure is ordered, and the order is the point of it.

Step 1 — always substitute first. Put the value straight into the expression. If what comes back is a well-defined expression, that is the limit and you stop; it does not matter whether the number is negative, fractional or ugly. She gives a whole slide to a case like this precisely so that nobody reaches for machinery before trying the obvious thing.

Step 2 — if substitution gives 0/0, look at what the expression is built out of, and let that choose the method.
 • Polynomials on top and bottom: factor both, cancel the common factor that was producing the zero, and substitute again.
 • A small fraction sitting inside the big fraction: multiply numerator and denominator by the common denominator to clear it, then factor; if the bracket that ought to cancel comes out reversed, take out a −1 so that it matches.
 • A square root in the expression: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator, which turns the root into a difference of squares and lets the offending factor cancel.

Step 3 — if none of those clears it, or if the expression contains something the algebra has no grip on, such as sin x or eˣ, replace f/g by f′/g′ — differentiating the two separately, not with the quotient rule — and re-check the form after each application. Apply it again if it is still 0/0 or ∞/∞, and stop as soon as it is not.

Two things to add. One of her TASKs needs two of these at once, so the methods are not exclusive alternatives: clearing an internal fraction can leave something that still needs factoring. And when a limit can be reached by two different routes, the two answers have to agree, which is a free check on the work.
why: Gives the procedure in her order — substitute first and stop if defined; then factor / clear the internal fraction / conjugate chosen by the visible feature; then L'Hôpital with the form re-checked after each application.

answer:
The rule she drills is: try the cheapest thing first, and only get the heavy tools out when the cheap thing fails.

Cheapest thing: just put the number in. If what comes back is an ordinary number — big, small, negative, a fraction, doesn't matter — you are finished, and you should not go looking for anything cleverer. People throw marks away reaching for a technique when the door was already open.

If putting the number in leaves you with nothing on top and nothing on the bottom, that is the signal to stop and look at what the thing is actually made of, because the ingredient tells you the tool.

If it is all ordinary powers of x, break both halves into brackets, throw away the bracket the two halves have in common, and put the number in again.

If there is a little fraction hiding inside the big one, wipe it out by multiplying the top and the bottom by the thing sitting underneath it, then break into brackets as before. If the bracket you want to throw away comes out the wrong way round, take a minus out the front and it lines up.

And if none of that touches it — or if the expression has a wave in it or a growth term that brackets cannot get hold of — then you take the slope of the top and the slope of the bottom, each on its own, and try again. Two more things. Sometimes one problem needs two of these back to back. And if you can reach the answer by two different roads and they meet, that is your marking scheme for free.

q: Explain why a definite integral never carries + c, and show the cancellation explicitly.
notes: A good answer performs the algebra rather than asserting the rule: take any antiderivative in the form F(x) + c; the theorem gives (F(b) + c) − (F(a) + c) = F(b) − F(a) + c − c = F(b) − F(a). It should then draw the consequence — every choice of c gives the same number, which is why the theorem can say 'if F(x) is an antiderivative' rather than 'the antiderivative', and why writing + c after a numerical answer is meaningless.
answer:
A definite integral never carries + c because the constant cancels itself in the evaluation, and you can watch it happen.

Let F(x) be an antiderivative of f(x). The whole family of antiderivatives is then F(x) + c, and the theorem says to evaluate that at the two limits and subtract:

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = [F(x) + c]ₐᵇ = (F(b) + c) − (F(a) + c)
   = F(b) + c − F(a) − c
   = F(b) − F(a).

The + c and the − c are the same constant, one added and one subtracted, so they annihilate each other and there is no trace of c left in the answer.

The consequence is worth stating. Because c drops out, every member of the family produces the same number, which is why the theorem can be phrased as 'if F(x) is an antiderivative of f' rather than 'the antiderivative' — you may take whichever one is convenient, in practice the one with c = 0, and the answer is unaffected. It is also why writing something like '12 + c' as the value of a definite integral is meaningless: what you are holding at the end is a single number, not a family of functions, and there is nothing left for c to be.

answer:
Because whatever you add to both ends gets taken straight back off again.

Picture measuring how much a plant grew between Monday and Friday. You can measure both heights up from the floor, or both up from the top of the table it is standing on. It makes no difference to the growth, because you take the Friday reading and subtract the Monday reading, and whatever offset you built into your measuring is sitting in both readings — once with a plus and once with a minus. It goes.

The same thing happens here. Whatever you found has some unknown lump added onto it, and you do not know what the lump is. Your top reading is (top value + lump) and your bottom reading is (bottom value + lump). Take one from the other and you get (top value + lump) − (bottom value + lump), which is top value + lump − bottom value − lump, which is just top value − bottom value. The lump has gone, and not because anyone decided to ignore it — it was subtracted from itself.

That is also why nobody has to tell you which version of the answer to use. Every version, whatever lump it happens to carry, spits out exactly the same number at the end, so you may as well use the one with no lump at all. And once you have done that subtraction you are holding a plain number. q: Explain why a definite integral never carries + c, and show the cancellation explicitly.
notes: A good answer performs the algebra rather than asserting the rule: take any antiderivative in the form F(x) + c; the theorem gives (F(b) + c) − (F(a) + c) = F(b) − F(a) + c − c = F(b) − F(a). answer:
A definite integral does not carry a constant of integration, and the reason lies in the essential difference between the two objects that the integral sign is used to denote.

The indefinite integral ∫f(x) dx denotes the complete family of antiderivatives of f. Since any two antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant, that family is written F(x) + c, with c an arbitrary real parameter. Here the constant is doing genuine work and is an indispensable part of the answer: without it, the expression names one single member of the family and thereby misrepresents the general solution, which is what the notation was asking for.

The definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is a different object altogether. It denotes a real number — on the standard interpretation, the signed area accumulated between the curve and the horizontal axis across the interval [a, b]. A number is not a family of functions, and it makes no sense to append an arbitrary parameter to a number. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus is precisely the bridge between the two objects: it tells us that this accumulated quantity can be recovered from an antiderivative evaluated at the two endpoints of the interval, and the output of that evaluation is fully determinate. The constant of integration, having had a real role in the indefinite case, simply has no role left to play once definite limits are imposed, and it is therefore correctly omitted. A student who writes a constant after a numerical answer has not yet distinguished the two objects from one another.

The choice between the disc, washer and shell methods is one of the central judgements in the study of solids of revolution, and each of the three is a fully rigorous means of computing the volume of such a solid.

The geometry of the region relative to the axis is what settles the matter, and a careful sketch will make the appropriate choice evident almost immediately. q: The vertical line test and the horizontal line test look almost identical but answer different questions. Explain what property each one is testing and why a graph can pass one and fail the other.
notes: The vertical line test checks whether each input has only one output - that is, whether the relation is a function at all. The horizontal line test checks whether each output comes from only one input - that is, whether the function is injective and therefore invertible. A graph can pass the first and fail the second: y = x^2 is a perfectly good function, since every x gives exactly one y, but the line y = 4 meets it twice, so two inputs share an output and it has no inverse on R. The two tests scan in perpendicular directions because they interrogate opposite halves of the pairing.
answer:
The two tests look alike but they interrogate opposite halves of the pairing between x and y.

The vertical line test asks whether each input has only one output. You sweep a vertical line across the graph; if it ever meets the curve in two or more places, then a single x value is paired with more than one y value, and the relation is not a function at all. So the vertical test is a test of whether you have a function in the first place.

The horizontal line test asks the reverse question: whether each output comes from only one input. You sweep a horizontal line across instead; if it meets the curve twice, then two different x values share the same y. The function is then not injective, and it has no inverse, because the inverse would have to send that shared output back to two different places at once, and no function is allowed to do that.

That is why a graph can pass one and fail the other. Take y = x². Every vertical line meets it exactly once — each x gives exactly one y — so it is a perfectly good function and passes the vertical test. But the horizontal line y = 4 meets it at x = −2 and at x = 2, so two inputs share an output, it fails the horizontal test, and on the whole of ℝ it has no inverse. The two tests scan in perpendicular directions precisely because one is checking the x → y direction of the pairing and the other the y → x direction, and those are separate conditions.
why: States both properties correctly — VLT for functionhood, HLT for injectivity and hence invertibility — and gives a valid example, y = x², that passes the first and fails the second at y = 4.

Think about a vending machine.

The first test is asking: when I press button 7, do I always get the same one thing out? If pressing 7 might hand you a Twix or might hand you a bag of crisps depending on its mood, then the machine is broken — that is not a proper machine at all. Sliding a vertical line across the picture is just pressing every button in turn and checking that each one has exactly one thing sitting behind it.

The second test asks a completely different question: if somebody hands me a Twix, can I tell which button they pressed? Sliding a horizontal line across is picking up each possible item and counting how many buttons will produce it. If two buttons both give you a Twix, then you cannot work backwards from the item to the button, and there is no way to build the reverse machine.

Those are plainly two different questions, so a machine can be perfectly fine on one and hopeless on the other. The squaring machine is the obvious case. q: The vertical line test and the horizontal line test look almost identical but answer different questions. Explain what property each one is testing and why a graph can pass one and fail the other.

answer:
The vertical and horizontal line tests are both graphical diagnostics: each consists of sweeping a straight line across the graph of a relation and counting the intersections it makes. Their similarity is entirely superficial, however, and the difference in their orientation is not accidental — it reflects the fact that they interrogate different aspects of the correspondence that a graph encodes between the two variables.

To apply the vertical line test, one imagines every vertical line x = k for k in the domain and asks how many times each of them meets the curve. The test is passed when no such line meets the curve more than once, and failed as soon as a single one does. To apply the horizontal line test, one does exactly the same thing with every horizontal line y = k, again counting intersections, and again passing only when no line meets the curve more than once. The two procedures are perfect mirror images of one another, differing solely in the direction of the sweep, which is precisely what makes them so easy for students to confuse.

The important conceptual point is that a graph carries two logically independent pieces of information about the relationship between its two variables, and each test is sensitive to exactly one of them and blind to the other. Because the properties they detect are independent, there is no implication in either direction between passing one and passing the other. A student must therefore always be clear about which of the two questions is actually being asked before deciding which line to sweep, since confusing them is among the most common errors at this stage of the course, and it can be avoided entirely by keeping firmly in mind that orientation and meaning go together.

q: Explain the sign convention behind emf = -N d(Phi)/dt: how the positive normal, the sign of the flux and the positive sense of circulation round the loop are tied together, and what the minus sign therefore asserts physically. Explain why 'the induced field opposes the applied field' is a wrong statement of Lenz's law, using the case of a decaying flux to show it.
notes: First choose a positive normal n for the loop - either face will do. The flux is then positive when B has a component along n and negative when it has one against. The positive sense of circulation round the loop is fixed by the right hand: curl the fingers in the positive sense of travel and the thumb must point along n. With those two choices locked together, emf = -N d(Phi)/dt gives an emf whose sign says which way it drives current: positive drives current in the positive circulation sense. Reverse the choice of n and both Phi and the positive sense reverse, so the emf reverses too, while the physical direction of current in the wire is unchanged - which is why the sign by itself is a convention. What is not a convention is the assertion the minus sign carries: whatever normal you pick, the induced current circulates so that its own flux through the loop opposes the change in Phi. Growing flux is fought by an opposing induced flux; shrinking flux is propped up by a reinforcing one. 'The induced field opposes the applied field' is therefore wrong: take a loop threaded by an into-page field that is decaying, so the change is a loss of into-page flux. The induced current must oppose that loss, so its own field inside the loop points into the page, the same way as B, not opposite to it. The corrupted rule gets that case backwards, and with it every withdrawal question, every falling-primary-current question, and the second half of the deck's galvanometer demonstration. The object of the opposition is always d(Phi)/dt, never B.
answer: The convention starts with a free choice: pick one face of the loop and call its outward direction the positive normal n. Either face will do — nothing physical depends on which. Once n is chosen, the sign of the flux is determined: Φ is positive when B has a component along n and negative when its component runs against n. The positive sense of circulation round the loop is then not free; it is locked to n by the right hand. Curl the fingers in the sense you are calling positive travel round the loop, and the thumb must lie along n. With both choices tied together in that way, emf = −N dΦ/dt yields a signed number whose sign is meaningful: a positive emf drives current in the positive circulation sense, a negative emf drives it the other way. Now the crucial point about what is and is not convention. Reverse the choice of n and three things reverse at once — the sign of Φ, the sign of dΦ/dt, and the positive circulation sense — so the emf changes sign, while the actual direction the current flows in the physical wire is completely unchanged. The sign, taken by itself, is therefore bookkeeping. What the minus sign asserts, and this survives any choice of normal, is a physical fact: the induced current always circulates so that the flux it produces through the loop opposes the change in Φ. Growing flux is fought by an induced flux the other way; shrinking flux is propped up by an induced flux the same way. Why 'the induced field opposes the applied field' is wrong. It substitutes B for dΦ/dt as the object of the opposition, and the two disagree whenever the flux is decaying. Take a loop threaded by a field into the page which is dying away. The change is a loss of into-page flux, and the induced current must oppose that loss, so it must try to maintain into-page flux — it circulates clockwise as seen from the front, and its own field inside the loop points into the page, the same way as the applied B, not against it. The corrupted rule predicts an out-of-page induced field and gets this case exactly backwards, and with it every question about withdrawing a magnet, opening a switch or a collapsing primary current. The opposition is always to the change in flux, never to the field itself.

q: For two positive charges of different size, the point where the resultant field vanishes always lies nearer the *smaller* charge. Explain why this must be so without doing the algebra, and state what changes about the location of the null point if one of the charges is made negative instead.
notes: At the null point the two field magnitudes are equal. The larger charge produces the stronger field at any given distance, so to be matched by the smaller charge's field it must be viewed from further away - which places the null point nearer the smaller charge, and between the two for like charges. If one charge is made negative the two contributions no longer oppose each other between the charges; they reinforce there, so no null point exists between them and it moves outside the pair, on the side of the smaller charge.
answer: At a null point the two fields must cancel, which requires their magnitudes to be equal and their directions opposite. Take the directions first. Between two positive charges the fields point away from each charge, hence towards each other, so between them is exactly where cancellation is possible; outside the pair both fields point the same way and can never cancel. So the null point lies between them. Now the magnitudes, with no algebra needed. Each charge's field weakens with distance in the same way, so at equal distances the larger charge always makes the stronger field. If the two fields are to be equal in size, the larger charge must be handicapped by distance and the smaller one favoured by it: you have to stand further from the larger charge than from the smaller. A point further from the larger and nearer the smaller is, by definition, a point nearer the smaller charge. Hence the null point must sit nearer the smaller charge — and this is forced by the shapes of the two curves alone, not by their algebraic details. If one charge is made negative instead, the direction argument reverses. Between the charges the field of the positive one points away from it and the field of the negative one points towards it, so between them the two contributions now point the same way and reinforce rather than oppose. There is therefore no null point between the charges at all. Cancellation is now only possible outside the pair, where the two fields oppose, and the equal-magnitude requirement still demands being further from the larger charge than from the smaller. So the null point moves out beyond the smaller charge, on the far side of it, outside the pair.
why: Pass: gives the mechanism (the larger charge must be viewed from further away to be matched) with no algebra, and correctly states that with one charge negative the null leaves the interior and lies outside the pair beyond the smaller charge.

For two like charges the null point is a genuine feature of the configuration and its position is determined entirely by the relative sizes of the two charges and by their separation, since these are the only parameters the problem contains. It is a well-established result, and one that can be confirmed by inspection of the field-line diagram, that this point always lies closer to the smaller of the two charges rather than the larger, and any answer placing it on the other side should be treated with suspicion. The field-line picture makes this vivid: the lines emerging from the two charges must meet somewhere, and the neutral point is where they do. If one of the charges is instead made negative, the configuration becomes a dipole-like arrangement of unequal magnitudes, and the entire field pattern is transformed — the lines no longer meet head-on but run from the positive charge to the negative one. q: Explain why the magnetic force does no work, and say exactly what is conserved as a result and what is not. Then explain why 'does no work' is not the same as 'exerts no force' and not the same as 'produces no acceleration'. Finish by explaining how a cyclotron nevertheless raises a proton's energy to many MeV.
notes: The magnetic force F = q*v cross B is perpendicular to both its factors, in particular perpendicular to v at every instant; work is the integral of F.dl with dl along v, so the integrand is identically zero and the instantaneous power P = F.v = 0. Hence the speed and the kinetic energy are exactly conserved however strong the field and however long the particle stays in it. What is not conserved is the momentum p = m*v, a vector whose direction turns continuously and reverses completely over half a revolution; nor is the velocity. 'Does no work' is not 'exerts no force': there is a real force of magnitude q*v*B, large enough to bend a proton beam round a 27 km ring. It is also not 'produces no acceleration': a = q*v*B/m is real and is what curves the path - a centripetal acceleration that changes the direction of v and not its magnitude, and confusing acceleration with speeding up is the error this topic exposes. A cyclotron therefore never uses the magnetic field to add energy. The field's job is to bend the protons round semicircles inside the dees and, because T = 2*pi*m/(qB) is independent of speed, to return them to the gap at strictly regular intervals. The energy comes entirely from the electric field across that gap: each crossing finds the alternating voltage reversed so that qE accelerates the proton again, adding qV of kinetic energy, and the radius grows as r = m*v/(qB) until after hundreds of crossings the proton spirals out at many MeV. Every joule came from E and none from B.
answer: Why no work. The magnetic force F = qv × B is perpendicular to both of its factors, and in particular perpendicular to v at every instant. Work is ∫F·dl with dl taken along the path, i.e. along v, so the integrand F·dl is identically zero, and the instantaneous power P = F·v = 0 at every moment. No integration over a complicated path is needed — the integrand never has a chance to be non-zero. What is and is not conserved. Since no work is done, the kinetic energy is exactly constant, and therefore so is the speed |v|, no matter how strong the field or how long the particle remains in it. What is not conserved is the velocity, whose direction turns continuously, and with it the momentum p = mv — a vector that swings right round and is exactly reversed after half a revolution. So: speed and kinetic energy conserved; velocity and momentum not. Not the same as 'exerts no force'. There is a perfectly real force of magnitude qvB. It is strong enough to hold a proton beam on a circular path round a 27 km ring; a force that did nothing could not do that. Doing no work means only that the force has no component along the motion, not that it is absent. Not the same as 'produces no acceleration'. Newton's second law gives a = qvB/m, a real acceleration, and it is precisely what curves the path. It is centripetal: it changes the direction of v while leaving |v| alone. The confusion here is between acceleration and speeding up — acceleration is a change of velocity, and a change of direction is a change of velocity. The cyclotron. It never uses B to supply energy, and could not. B has two jobs: it bends the protons round semicircles inside the hollow dees, and because the period T = 2πm/(qB) is independent of both speed and radius, it delivers them back to the gap at strictly regular intervals, in step with a fixed-frequency oscillator. All the energy comes from the electric field across that gap. The alternating voltage is arranged to have reversed by the time the proton arrives, so every crossing finds a field that accelerates it, adding qV of kinetic energy each time. The radius then grows as r = mv/(qB), the proton spirals outwards, and after hundreds of crossings it emerges at many MeV. Every joule of that came from E and none of it from B.

answer: Think of a rope tied to a stone you are whirling round your head. The rope pulls sideways to the way the stone is travelling, never forwards along it. If a pull is always sideways it can never help the stone along or hold it back, so it never feeds it or drains it. Magnetism does the same thing to a moving charge: the shove it gives is always square to the way the thing is going, at every instant, so the running total of energy handed over is zero from start to finish. What follows is that the thing keeps exactly the speed it came in with, forever, and the energy stored in that speed never budges — no matter how ferocious the magnet or how long it stays in there. What does not stay put is which way it is going, and therefore the combination of how heavy it is with which way and how fast it is going. Do half a loop and that combination is pointing the exact opposite way from where it started. So: how fast, unchanged; which way, changing the whole time. Now, two things people slide into which are simply not the same as what I just said. First, none of this says there is no shove. There absolutely is, and it is a hefty one — it is stiff enough to steer a beam of protons round a ring the size of a small city and keep it there. A shove that gives no energy is still a shove. Second, none of it says the thing is not being pulled off its straight line. It is, constantly. That is the whole point — the sideways pull is exactly what makes the path bend into a circle instead of running off straight. People trip over the word because they hear it as getting quicker, but changing which way you are pointing counts every bit as much as changing how fast you are moving. Which brings me to the machine that whirls protons up to enormous energies. The magnet in it is not what feeds them, and could not be, for everything I just said. The magnet does two jobs and only two: it curls them round half-circles inside the two hollow D-shaped boxes, and — this is the clever part — the time to go round is the same whatever the speed, so they keep coming back to the slot between the boxes on a completely steady beat. That lets a plain fixed-rhythm voltage supply do the feeding. Every time a proton crosses the slot, the voltage has flipped over in time to shove it forward, so it picks up a bite of energy at every crossing. Going faster makes the half-circles wider, so it works its way outwards in a spiral, and after several hundred passes it comes out with an enormous amount of energy. Every scrap of that came from the voltage across the slot. The magnet contributed steering and timekeeping and not one bit of energy.

The magnetic force on a moving charge is given by F = qv × B, a relation whose vector-product structure is unlike anything in the electrostatic case and which repays careful study. From this structure follows the celebrated no-work theorem, which states that the magnetic force does no work on a charged particle whatever its trajectory and whatever the configuration of the field — a result so general that it holds for uniform and non-uniform fields alike, and one of the cornerstones of the subject. The energetic consequences of this theorem are far-reaching and must be thought through with care, since the conserved and non-conserved quantities in the problem are not the ones a casual reading would suggest, and precision about which is which is what separates a secure understanding from a superficial one. It is equally essential to distinguish the no-work theorem from two propositions with which it is routinely and unfortunately confused, namely the claim that the magnetic force is somehow not a real force, and the claim that it produces no acceleration. Both confusions are widespread, both are serious, and both dissolve the moment the Lorentz force law is read properly. A student who conflates these three distinct statements will make errors throughout the whole of magnetism, and examiners see the consequences every year. The cyclotron provides the perfect illustration of the principle in action. Invented by Lawrence, it accelerates protons through hundreds of successive passes to energies of many MeV, exploiting the remarkable fact that the cyclotron period T = 2πm/(qB) is independent of the particle's speed — a property without which the whole design would be impossible and which is directly traceable to the structure of the Lorentz force.
